RQ1 Amendments: Structural Change at the Attributed Balancing Margin

A cumulative new results section implementing supervisor amendments while preserving the canonical RQ1 and unified reports as separate audit artefacts.

Study window: 1 January 2023–31 December 2025 · Generated 20 July 2026, 12:29 GMT Daylight Time · Amendment artefact
12quarters
2active-side regimes
6primary evidence figures
24validated side-quarters

1. The question this figure answers

How did the technology composition of the attributed balancing margin change between 2023 and 2025 on the bid and offer sides?

The pooled 2023–2025 averages remain correct, but they flatten the transition from batteries being peripheral in early 2023 to forming roughly one-third of the attributed margin by late 2025. This amendment therefore treats speed, direction and crossover as the principal evidence.

2. Primary visual evidence

Quarterly technology trajectories by active side

Figure A1.1. Panel A shows battery, CCGT and wind in long-system, bid-active periods. Panel B shows battery, CCGT and pumped storage in short-system, offer-active periods. Shares use all valid attributed marginal weight within each side-quarter; displayed technologies are not renormalised.

Evidence

  • Bid-side battery share increased from 0.8% in 2023 Q1 to 36.2% in 2025 Q4.
  • Bid-side CCGT declined from 54.8% to 33.6%; battery first exceeded it in 2025 Q3 and remained ahead in Q4.
  • Offer-side battery increased from 3.2% to 26.9%, while pumped storage declined from 33.3% to 10.4%.
  • All observed technologies remain in each side-quarter denominator; the displayed series are not renormalised around the focal technologies.
Main result.

On the bid side, battery increased from 0.8% to 36.2%, while CCGT declined from 54.8% to 33.6%. Battery first exceeded CCGT in 2025 Q3. On the offer side, battery increased from 3.2% to 26.9%, pumped storage declined from 33.3% to 10.4%, and CCGT ended at 45.0%.

3. Commentary and analysis

Bid-active, long-system transition

Battery and CCGT shares converged and crossed, while wind retained volatile, episodic importance during some surplus periods. The crossover is the clearest evidence that the period-wide composition was not stationary.

Offer-active, short-system transition

Battery growth occurred alongside a substantial decline in pumped-storage representation, while CCGT remained comparatively persistent. The common battery direction therefore masks a different surrounding technological transition from that observed on the bid side.

Interpretive boundary. These trajectories establish changing representation at the attributed margin. They do not identify causal displacement, a technology-specific price effect, or behavioural change per BMU or per GW.

4. Calculation, method and limitations

  1. Sum tie-adjusted marginal weight attributed to each technology in every active-side quarter.
  2. Divide by all valid marginal weight in that side-quarter.
  3. Express the result as a percentage.

Each Settlement Period contributes one unit divided across any co-marginal BMUs. All observed technologies remain in the denominator, including those omitted from the focused chart. Battery fleet capacity and the number of commissioned BMUs expanded during the study period, so the chart is not capacity-adjusted.

5. Capacity growth and the question of marginal capture intensity

Did battery marginality rise only because more fleet capacity existed, or did the operational fleet capture the attributed margin more intensively?

The preceding figure establishes a sharp increase in battery marginal share. This second analysis introduces operational power, energy and asset counts so that growth in the fleet can be separated from growth in marginal representation per unit of fleet scale.

6. Capacity and capacity-normalised evidence

Battery fleet growth and marginal capture intensity

Figure A1.2. Panels A and B describe the operational battery fleet. Panels C and D divide tie-adjusted battery marginal weight by operational fleet scale and by all active-side Settlement Period weight, reporting attributed battery marginal periods per GW or asset for every 1,000 active-side periods.

Evidence

  • Operational power increased from 2.45 GW to 6.50 GW; energy capacity increased from 2.85 GWh to 10.37 GWh.
  • The operational fleet expanded from 90 to 187 assets, while implied average duration increased from 1.16 to 1.60 hours.
  • Bid-side normalised marginal capture rose from 3.2 to 55.6 attributed marginal periods per GW per 1,000 bid-active periods.
  • Offer-side normalised marginal capture rose from 13.0 to 41.4 per GW per 1,000 offer-active periods.
  • The corresponding per-asset rate increased from 0.09 to 1.93 on bids and from 0.35 to 1.44 on offers.

7. Interpretation, calculation and limitations

Interpretation

  • Total battery marginal share and the normalised per-GW rate both increased on each active side. The growth in marginal representation therefore outpaced the growth in installed power over the study endpoints.
  • The bid-side increase was especially pronounced, although its percentage change is magnified by the very low 2023 Q1 starting value.
  • The per-asset results point in the same direction, so the conclusion is not an artefact of using power capacity rather than asset count as the fleet denominator.
  • The evidence supports increased marginal capture intensity or competitive positioning at the attributed margin. It does not establish improved profitability.

Calculation

Primary normalised measure.

Tie-adjusted battery marginal weight ÷ operational battery GW ÷ all active-side Settlement Period weight × 1,000. The asset-normalised version replaces GW with the operational asset count.

The audit CSV additionally reports battery marginal share per GW, raw attributed marginal periods per GW, and the corresponding three measures per operational asset. Capacity values are preserved exactly from the supervisor-supplied quarterly table; the analysis uses 2023 Q1–2025 Q4 to match the dissertation window.

Interpretive boundary. Fleet-average measures do not control for commissioning date within a quarter, connection constraints, cycling limits, state of charge, availability, degradation, ownership strategy or BM participation eligibility. They describe aggregate marginal capture, not unit economics, revenue or causal cannibalisation.

8. Exploratory capacity–marginality relationship

How closely did quarterly battery marginal shares move with operational battery power capacity?

Figure A1.1 establishes the timing of the market transition. Figure A1.3 recasts the same quarterly battery shares against operational power capacity, while Figure A1.2 Panel C remains the direct time-series test of fleet-level marginal capture per GW.

Operational battery power capacity and quarterly battery marginal share

Figure A1.3. Each observation is one quarter from 2023 Q1 to 2025 Q4. Lines are simple OLS fits and shaded areas are 95% confidence intervals for the fitted mean. Labels identify 2023 Q1, 2024 Q1, 2025 Q1 and 2025 Q4.

Evidence

  • Within the 2023–2025 quarterly sample, each additional GW of operational battery power was associated with 9.11 percentage points more bid-side marginal share and 7.08 percentage points more offer-side share.
  • For bids (n = 12), Pearson r = 0.98, Spearman ρ = 0.99, and R2 = 0.95. For offers (n = 12), Pearson r = 0.94, Spearman ρ = 0.96, and R2 = 0.89.
  • The selected quarter labels expose the chronology behind the fitted relationship rather than presenting the points as independent cross-sectional observations.
  • The direct capacity-normalised series in Figure A1.2 Panel C shows whether marginal capture per GW strengthened or weakened over time; it is more informative than the regression alone for that question.
Non-causal exploratory result. Capacity and marginal share both trend through time, and the twelve quarterly observations are serially ordered. The fitted relationship is descriptive: it does not prove that added battery capacity caused the change in marginal share. The negative fitted intercepts only position the lines within the observed capacity range; they have no economic interpretation and the models must not be extrapolated towards zero capacity.

9. Exploratory statistics and incumbent comparisons

Pearson correlation summarises the linear relationship; Spearman correlation tests whether the ordering is consistently monotonic. The slope and simple linear R2 describe the fitted quarterly association. The main table deliberately omits p-values: exact inferential statistics and standard errors remain in the audit appendix.

  • Capacity versus CCGT bid share: Pearson r = -0.83, Spearman ρ = -0.88, slope = -7.36 percentage points per GW, and R2 = 0.69.
  • Capacity versus pumped-storage offer share: Pearson r = -0.90, Spearman ρ = -0.92, slope = -5.99 percentage points per GW, and R2 = 0.81.
  • Capacity versus CCGT offer share: Pearson r = -0.54, Spearman ρ = -0.55, slope = -2.35 percentage points per GW, and R2 = 0.29.
  • Among the three requested incumbent comparisons, the largest absolute Pearson association is for Pumped-storage offer share (r = -0.90). This identifies the incumbent trajectory that most closely mirrors battery capacity growth; it is not evidence of technological displacement.

10. Main linear models

Separate ordinary least-squares models are estimated for the bid and offer sides. Marginal share is measured in percentage points and operational battery capacity in GW. HC3 standard errors are used to reduce sensitivity to heteroskedasticity and influential observations in this twelve-quarter sample; confidence intervals and p-values use the residual t distribution with 10 degrees of freedom.

Battery marginality

Model 1A.

Battery bid share = constant + operational battery capacity.

Model 1B.

Battery offer share = constant + operational battery capacity.

Within the 2023–2025 quarterly sample, each additional GW of operational battery power was associated with an estimated 9.11-percentage-point increase in bid-side marginal share and a 7.08-percentage-point increase in offer-side marginal share.

Model 1B Battery offer share 7.083 [4.45, 9.72] p<0.001 0.887 0.875 12 3.393

Model 2B Pumped-storage offer share -5.989 [-8.85, -3.12] p<0.001 0.815 0.796 12 3.831

Evidence

  • Model 1A reports 9.11 percentage points per GW, with a 95% HC3 interval from 7.76 to 10.45; R2 = 0.951, adjusted R2 = 0.946, and residual standard error = 2.76 percentage points.
  • Model 1B reports 7.08 percentage points per GW, with a 95% HC3 interval from 4.45 to 9.72; R2 = 0.887, adjusted R2 = 0.875, and residual standard error = 3.39 percentage points.

Incumbent-share models

Models 2A–2C estimate CCGT bid share, pumped-storage offer share and CCGT offer share separately against operational battery capacity.

  • CCGT bid share was associated with a 7.36-percentage-point decline per additional GW of operational battery capacity; the 95% HC3 interval is -12.05 to -2.67 and R2 = 0.686.
  • Pumped-storage offer share was associated with a 5.99-percentage-point decline per additional GW; the interval is -8.85 to -3.12 and R2 = 0.815.
  • CCGT offer share had a smaller and less precisely estimated association: -2.35 percentage points per GW, with an interval from -4.85 to 0.14 and R2 = 0.287.
Interpretive boundary. These coefficients quantify compositional associations within twelve serially ordered quarters. They do not show that battery capacity caused incumbent displacement. P-values are reported for completeness but do not carry the argument; coefficient magnitude, uncertainty, model fit and the diagnostics below are more informative.

11. Model diagnostics and specification decision

Decision.

The simple linear model remains the transparent headline specification, but only as a descriptive levels relationship. The first-difference and time-trend checks show that the high levels R2 should not be interpreted as independent evidence that capacity additions caused higher marginal share.

First differences

  • Bid-side quarterly changes (n = 11) produced a slope of -9.43 percentage points per GW, Pearson r = -0.42, Spearman ρ = -0.42, and R2 = 0.18.
  • Offer-side quarterly changes (n = 11) produced a slope of -13.86, Pearson r = -0.58, Spearman ρ = -0.50, and R2 = 0.34.
  • The strong positive levels relationships therefore do not persist in quarter-to-quarter changes. This indicates that their high R2 values are largely associated with the shared long-term trend.

Time-trend sensitivity

  • Operational capacity and the quarter index correlate at r = 0.994, giving a variance-inflation factor of 84.0.
  • After including a linear quarter trend, the capacity coefficient becomes 1.63 percentage points per GW for bids and -10.54 for offers.
  • The extreme collinearity makes those conditional coefficients unstable. The twelve-quarter sample cannot cleanly distinguish fleet expansion from other changes occurring through time.

Leave-one-quarter-out stability

  • The bid slope ranges from 8.74 to 9.39, with a median of 9.11 percentage points per GW.
  • The offer slope ranges from 6.66 to 8.14, with a median of 7.05.
  • The direction never changes on either side, so no single quarter—including 2025 Q3 or Q4—drives the positive levels association.

HC3 versus one-lag HAC uncertainty

HC3 addresses leverage and heteroskedasticity; the one-lag Newey–West HAC estimator additionally allows adjacent-quarter residual dependence. The HAC calculation uses a Bartlett lag-one weight and the finite-sample correction n/(n−k).

Model Outcome Lag-1 residual r HC3 SE HAC(1) SE HAC/HC3 SE ratio 95% HC3 interval 95% HAC(1) interval
Model 1A Battery bid share -0.225 0.602 0.443 0.735 [7.76, 10.45] [8.12, 10.09]
Model 1B Battery offer share -0.035 1.183 0.744 0.629 [4.45, 9.72] [5.43, 8.74]
Model 2A CCGT bid share -0.026 2.105 1.617 0.768 [-12.05, -2.67] [-10.96, -3.76]
Model 2B Pumped-storage offer share -0.475 1.286 0.912 0.709 [-8.85, -3.12] [-8.02, -3.96]
Model 2C CCGT offer share -0.192 1.120 0.723 0.645 [-4.85, 0.14] [-3.96, -0.74]
  • For battery bid share, the slope standard error is 0.602 under HC3 and 0.443 under HAC(1); the HAC/HC3 ratio is 0.74.
  • For battery offer share, the corresponding standard errors are 1.183 and 0.744, giving a ratio of 0.63.
  • Across all five models, lag-one residual correlations range from -0.47 to -0.03 and HAC(1)-to-HC3 standard-error ratios range from 0.63 to 0.77. The non-positive residual dependence makes every HAC(1) interval narrower than its HC3 counterpart.
  • The CCGT offer interval excludes zero under HAC(1) but not under HC3. That estimator-sensitive distinction is not used to strengthen the substantive claim: HC3 remains the primary small-sample uncertainty specification, and HAC(1) is reported as sensitivity evidence.

Linear versus quadratic

  • For bids, linear AICc is 31.20 versus 34.95 for quadratic; leave-one-out RMSE is 2.95 versus 3.06 percentage points.
  • For offers, linear AICc is 36.13 versus 38.90; leave-one-out RMSE is 3.93 versus 4.30.
  • The quadratic does not improve AICc or out-of-sample error on either side, and offer-side curvature changes direction across leave-one-quarter-out fits. The additional term is therefore rejected.

12. Conditional scenario analysis at 8–10 GW

If the selected 2023–2025 linear relationships continued, what battery marginal shares would be conditionally fitted at 8, 9 and 10 GW?

The scenario analysis follows model selection and stability testing. The linear specification is retained because the quadratic did not improve AICc or leave-one-out RMSE. However, the largest observed quarterly capacity was 6.50 GW, so every scenario below is outside the estimation range.

Conditional extrapolation beyond the observed battery-capacity range

Figure A1.4. Solid fitted lines cover the observed 2023–2025 capacity range; dashed lines extend the selected linear models to 10 GW. Coloured bands are 95% confidence intervals for the conditional mean using HC3 coefficient covariance. Wider grey bands are 95% prediction intervals after adding historical residual variation.

Active-side outcome Scenario capacity (GW) Conditional fitted share (%) 95% HC3 confidence interval 95% prediction interval
Battery bid share 8 49.8 [44.4, 55.2] [41.6, 58.0]
Battery bid share 9 58.9 [52.3, 65.5] [49.9, 68.0]
Battery bid share 10 68.0 [60.1, 75.9] [58.0, 78.0]
Battery offer share 8 43.4 [32.2, 54.6] [29.9, 56.9]
Battery offer share 9 50.5 [36.7, 64.3] [34.7, 66.2]
Battery offer share 10 57.6 [41.1, 74.0] [39.5, 75.6]

Evidence

  • At 8 GW, the conditional fitted share is 49.8% for bids and 43.4% for offers.
  • At 9 GW, the fitted share is 58.9% for bids and 50.5% for offers.
  • At 10 GW, it reaches 68.0% for bids and 57.6% for offers, conditional on the historical slopes continuing.
  • Uncertainty expands beyond the observed limit: at 10 GW, the bid-side 95% prediction interval is 58.0% to 78.0%, and the offer-side interval is 39.5% to 75.6%.
Conditional extrapolations—not forecasts. These scenarios assume that the 2023–2025 association persists despite increasing battery competition, possible market saturation, changing duration, rule changes, different system conditions, and continued CCGT and pumped-storage responses. They do not model those mechanisms. No quadratic extrapolation is used.

13. Yearly System Price distributions by marginal technology

Did the pooled 2023–2025 technology-conditioned price distributions conceal changes in central prices or directional tails between years?

The original pooled two-panel figure is retained as a separate canonical audit artefact. Figure A1.5 replaces pooling in the amendments narrative with aligned yearly panels, preserving the same one-observation-per-Settlement-Period–technology construction and the same directionally relevant quantiles.

Year-specific technology-conditioned System Price distributions

Figure A1.5. Columns separate 2023, 2024 and 2025; rows separate bid-active and offer-active periods. Thick bars show the interquartile range and open circles the median. Bid panels extend to P10 and P5; offer panels extend to P90 and P95. All panels share a common price axis.

Evidence

  • Battery’s bid-active median was £57.80/MWh in 2023, £52.15/MWh in 2024 and £62.02/MWh in 2025. Its bid-side P5 moved from £6.99/MWh to £-6.42/MWh and £-10.98/MWh, exposing a negative-price tail that the pooled interval softens.
  • Battery’s offer-active median fell from £131.40/MWh in 2023 to £102.00/MWh in 2024, before recovering partly to £106.29/MWh in 2025. Its P95 followed the same broad pattern: £200.00, £134.78 and £145.89/MWh.
  • Pumped storage’s offer-side P95 declined from £219.89/MWh to £128.00/MWh, then rose to £154.80/MWh. The pooled upper tail therefore combines a high-price 2023 regime with materially lower later-year outcomes.
  • Wind’s bid-side P5 was £-74.00/MWh in 2023, compared with £-44.76/MWh in 2024 and £-43.79/MWh in 2025. Wind remained associated with the most negative directional bid tail, but the 2023 extreme was not representative of every year.
Interpretive boundary. These are descriptive conditional distributions, not technology effects. Yearly splitting also exposes sparse cells: wind has only 10, 6 and 17 offer-active marginal periods in 2023, 2024 and 2025. Quantiles for such cells are shown for audit completeness but should not carry substantive comparisons.

14. Technology composition and System Price across NIV intensity

How did the composition of the attributed margin change with the direction and severity of system imbalance?

This figure is carried forward from the previous RQ1 HTML because it connects the technology-transition narrative to system conditions. Symmetric NIV bins distinguish increasingly long, bid-active periods from increasingly short, offer-active periods; column headers retain median System Price and the number of valid Settlement Periods.

Marginal technology composition across NIV direction and intensity

Figure A1.6. Heatmap cells show each displayed technology’s tie-adjusted share of attributed marginal Settlement Period weight within each NIV bin. Seven principal technologies are displayed; omitted technologies remain in each bin’s denominator, so visible shares may sum to less than 100%. NIV is measured in MWh per Settlement Period.

Evidence

  • Wind’s share rises to 52.5% in the most extreme long-system bin, compared with 7.8% close to balance and 0.0% in the most extreme short-system bin.
  • CCGT increases from 8.3% in the outer long-system bin to 48.8% near balance on the bid side. On the offer side it accounts for 48.6% near balance and 33.2% in the outer short-system bin.
  • Battery representation increases across the short-system bins from 16.2% to 25.4%, while pumped storage rises from 17.5% to 22.7% before falling to 12.3% in the outermost bin.
  • Median System Price moves from £-25/MWh in the most extreme long-system bin to £128/MWh in the most extreme short-system bin, linking imbalance direction to markedly different price regimes.
Interpretive boundary. The two outer bins contain only 265 and 138 Settlement Periods. Their composition estimates are descriptively informative but less stable than the central bins. The heatmap reports conditional representation, not causal dispatch or price effects.
